performance_optimizations.title: Fix N+1 Query in Material Search API
performance_optimizations.description: The `material_search_api()` endpoint iterates through materials and calls `material.get_best_price()` for each one, triggering a separate database query per material. This creates an N+1 query pattern where 10 search results generate 11 queries (1 main + 10 per-material).
performance_optimizations.rationale: This API endpoint is called on every keystroke for material autocomplete searches. With typical usage patterns of 2-3 searches per form interaction, this could generate 30+ database queries per user action. The fix is straightforward with `Prefetch` and annotation.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: N+1 queries: 11 queries for 10 results, ~100ms response time under load
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: Single query with annotation, reduce to 1 query, ~10ms response time
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Use Django's annotate() with Min() to get best price in the main query
2. Replace: `materials = Material.objects.filter(...)` with `materials = Material.objects.filter(...).annotate(best_price=Min('materialsupplier__price_per_kg', filter=Q(materialsupplier__supplier__is_active=True)))`
3. Access `material.best_price` instead of calling `material.get_best_price()`
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Slight increase in main query complexity, but net reduction in total query time

performance_optimizations.title: Add Redis Caching for Dashboard Statistics
performance_optimizations.description: Dashboard views (materials/dashboard, inventory/dashboard, production stats) compute aggregate statistics on every page load using COUNT, SUM, and other aggregations. These queries run on potentially large tables without any caching.
performance_optimizations.rationale: Redis is already configured in docker-compose but not utilized in Django. Dashboard statistics rarely change and are perfect candidates for caching. Multiple users viewing dashboards amplify the database load unnecessarily.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: 6-8 aggregate queries per dashboard load, ~200-400ms per request
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: 0 queries for cached requests, ~5ms cache lookup, 95%+ cache hit rate
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Add Django cache configuration for Redis in settings.py
2. Import cache: `from django.core.cache import cache`
3. Wrap stats computation: `stats = cache.get('dashboard_stats') or compute_and_cache()`
4. Set 60-second TTL for stats
5. Invalidate cache on relevant model signals (post_save, post_delete)
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Stats may be up to 60 seconds stale; requires cache invalidation strategy

performance_optimizations.title: Remove Unused Static File Plugins to Reduce Deployment Size
performance_optimizations.description: The staticfiles/plugins directory contains ~50MB of unused JavaScript libraries (DataTables extensions, CKEditor, Flot charts, etc.) that were likely part of an admin template. The actual application only uses Tabler, HTMX, and Alpine.js which are in static/vendor/.
performance_optimizations.rationale: Large static file directories slow down `collectstatic`, increase deployment image size, and waste storage. The unused plugins also pose security risks if they contain outdated vulnerable code. The base template confirms only Tabler/HTMX/Alpine are loaded.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: ~50MB of static files, ~30 unused JavaScript plugins
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: ~45MB reduction, faster deployments, smaller Docker images
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Audit staticfiles/ vs static/ to confirm which are used
2. Create backup of staticfiles/plugins/
3. Remove unused plugins: DataTables, CKEditor, Flot, Morris charts, etc.
4. Remove legacy IE compatibility files (html5shiv, respond.js, excanvas)
5. Remove *.demo.min.js files
6. Run collectstatic to verify no missing assets
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Need to verify no templates reference these files before removal

performance_optimizations.title: Add Database Indexes for Frequently Filtered Fields
performance_optimizations.description: Several Django models filter on fields that lack explicit database indexes. Fields like `status`, `movement_type`, `is_active`, and date fields are used in WHERE clauses and ordering but rely on implicit indexing or full table scans.
performance_optimizations.rationale: List views filter by status (DRAFT, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED), movement_type (IN, OUT, TRANSFER), and date ranges. As data grows, these queries will become slower without proper indexes. PostgreSQL's query planner needs hints for optimal paths.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: Sequential scans on status/type filters with large datasets
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: Index-only scans, 10-100x faster filtering on 10k+ records
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Add db_index=True to frequently filtered fields:
   - ProductionOrder.status
   - Batch.status
   - StockMovement.movement_type
   - StockMovement.created_at
   - InventoryCount.status
2. Create migration with `python manage.py makemigrations`
3. Apply migration with `python manage.py migrate`
4. Consider composite indexes for common filter combinations
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Indexes add write overhead and storage; only add for truly hot paths

performance_optimizations.title: Avoid Duplicate .count() Queries in List Views
performance_optimizations.description: List views like `material_list()`, `supplier_list()`, and `stock_list()` call `.count()` on filtered querysets and also pass the same queryset to Paginator. Django's Paginator internally calls `.count()` again, resulting in duplicate COUNT queries.
performance_optimizations.rationale: Each duplicate COUNT query adds 50-100ms on large tables. This pattern appears in at least 5 list views. The fix is simple: use paginator.count instead of calling queryset.count() separately.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: 2 COUNT queries per list page load instead of 1
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: 50% reduction in COUNT queries, ~50ms saved per page load
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Remove standalone `.count()` calls like `'total_materials': materials.count()`
2. Use paginator properties instead:
   ```python
   paginator = Paginator(materials, 20)
   page_obj = paginator.get_page(page_number)
   # Instead of materials.count(), use:
   context['total_materials'] = paginator.count
   ```
3. Apply pattern across all list views
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: None - purely beneficial change with no downsides
